title: The Gosinga grove
hookLine: which monk would light up the grove? each answers from his own practice

lines: A FULL MOON, THE SAL TREES IN BLOOM.
WHO WOULD LIGHT UP THIS GROVE?
cards: It's a clear night with the moon full. The sal trees are in bloom, and the text says the whole wood smells as if heavenly scents were drifting through it.

Six of the Buddha's great disciples have gathered in the Gosinga grove. Sariputta looks around and asks the others a question that sounds almost like a parlor game: what kind of monk would light up this grove?
Everyone answers. Nobody gives the same answer.

teach.h: SIX ANSWERS UNDER A FULL MOON
teach.b: This is the greater discourse in Gosinga, the thirty-second of the Middle-Length Sayings. Ananda, who memorized the teachings, says: a monk who has learned much, remembers it, and teaches it clearly.
Revata says: a monk who delights in solitary meditation. Anuruddha, known for his inner sight, says: a monk who sees a thousand worlds with the divine eye.
Mahakassapa, the strict forest monk, says: one who lives in the forest, eats only alms food, wears rag robes, wants little, and praises those things to others.
Moggallana says: two monks discussing the teaching deeply, asking and answering without faltering.

And Sariputta says: a monk who masters his own mind, who can rest in whatever state he chooses in the morning, at noon or at evening, like a king with a chest full of clothes who wears whatever color he likes.

teach.h: EACH NAMES THE PRACTICE HE LOVES
teach.b: Each one names his own practice. That's not vanity; it's honesty. You can only praise what you actually love.
Then they go to the Buddha and ask: who spoke best?
All of you spoke well, he says, each in your own way.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA: SIT UNTIL THE MIND IS FREE
teach.b: Then he gives his own answer: a monk who sits down after his meal, legs crossed, body straight, determined not to get up until his mind is free. He doesn't rank them.
A community is lit by many lamps, and the light is different from each one: the learner, the hermit, the seer, the ascetic, the debater, the master of mind. One grove.

how: Buddhist traditions honor many temperaments of practice, from study and teaching to forest asceticism and meditation, and MN 32 is often taught as a picture of a community where each kind of practitioner has a place.

o: a hill where the Buddha gave his first talk
a moonlit grove lit by six disciples
a holy cow honored at a temple gate

games.q: who lights the grove how — tap the pairs.
p: learned much, and teaches it clearly
forest, alms food, rag robes, few wants
masters his mind, like a king's wardrobe

s: the Buddha chose one answer as the best
he said all of them spoke well, each in their own way, and then gave his own.
each disciple named the practice he himself was known for
Ananda praised learning, Revata solitude, Anuruddha the divine eye, and so on.
the conversation happened on a moonlit night with sal trees in bloom
the text sets it in the Gosinga wood on a clear night, the trees flowering.

games.q: six disciples come to you, each with a different answer to the question 'who would light up this grove?' they ask which one is best. you're the Buddha. what do you say?
o: all of you spoke well, each in your own way.
none of you; only I light the grove.
games.why: the Buddha affirms every answer, and then adds his own: a monk who sits determined not to rise until his mind is free.

practice: Ask yourself Sariputta's question: not what should light your grove, but what actually does, for you.

Learning something and understanding it, quiet time alone, wanting less, a good conversation, a steady mind: let one answer come, and don't argue with it. Then sit the way the Buddha described, body straight, settled, simply here.

wordCard.voice: Gosinga. A wood of blooming sal trees, a full moon, and six disciples who each light it in their own way.

orig.note: Pali gosinga: cow's horn (go, cow + singa, horn), the name of the sal-tree wood.

carryVoice: Your line: each lights it differently. Six lamps, and the Buddha didn't rank them. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 32, Mahagosinga Sutta (the greater discourse in Gosinga)
